The idea of this topic is that there is no one formula per figure to memorise, but a single one — the rectangle's, counting little squares — and a method for reducing the others to it. The circle is the only one that will not be cut up, and out of that comes the number $\pi$.

Land-registry and design programs do the same, only with thousands of triangles a second.
La circunferencia y el número π: The circle and the number π
Si mides el contorno de cualquier objeto: If you measure the outline of any round object and divide it by its diameter, the same number always comes out. It makes no difference whether it is a coin or the orbit of Jupiter. That number is $\pi$.
Arquímedes (siglo III a.C.) acorraló a $: Archimedes (third century BC) cornered $\pi$ by trapping the circle between two regular polygons, one inscribed and one circumscribed, and kept doubling the sides until he reached 96. That way he proved that $\frac{223}{71} < \pi < \frac{22}{7}$, that is, between 3.1408 and 3.1429. In 1761 Lambert proved that $\pi$ is irrational, and in 1882 Lindemann that it is transcendental: it is not a solution of any polynomial equation with whole-number coefficients. That closed at a stroke the problem of squaring the circle, open for two thousand years.

It appears in the period of a pendulum, in the formula of the normal distribution that governs errors of measurement and in any phenomenon that oscillates, because everything that turns or repeats ends up passing through a circle. NASA works out interplanetary trajectories with fifteen decimal places of $\pi$: with that, the error in measuring the Earth's orbit is smaller than the thickness of a hair.
